ground_truth.description: The init() function lacks access control and initialization guards, allowing repeated calls that overwrite the builderAdmin state variable. Attacker calls init(attacker_address) to seize admin, then sweep() to drain funds.
ground_truth.root_cause: The init() function lacks access control and initialization guards, allowing repeated calls that overwrite the builderAdmin state variable. Attacker calls init(attacker_address) to seize admin, then sweep() to drain funds.
ground_truth.attack_scenario: 1) Builder wallet deployed and accumulates fees. 2) Attacker calls init(attacker) to become admin. 3) Attacker calls sweep(token, attacker) to extract all balances.
ground_truth.fix_description: Implement access control on init() and add an initialization guard (require(!initialized)) to ensure single execution.

vulnerabilities.type: Unprotected initializer allows takeover of fee-recipient wallet
vulnerabilities.explanation: BuilderWallet uses a two-step initialization pattern, but `init(address _builderAdmin)` is `external` and has no access control and no “only-once” guard. Therefore, *anyone* can call `init` at any time to overwrite `builderAdmin`. Since `sweep()` authorizes solely by `msg.sender == builderAdmin`, an attacker can take over any deployed BuilderWallet and steal all tokens held by it (e.g., protocol/builder fee distributions sent to the deterministic wallet address computed from a builder code). This does not require compromising the RiskEngine guardian or the BuilderFactory owner; it only requires knowing the wallet address (predictable by CREATE2 / builderCode).
vulnerabilities.attack_scenario:
1) Identify a builderCode used by the protocol (or observe feeRecipient addresses on-chain).
2) Compute the corresponding BuilderWallet address (or just read it from events/transactions).
3) Call `BuilderWallet.init(attackerEOA)` from the attacker account to set `builderAdmin` to the attacker.
4) Call `BuilderWallet.sweep(token, attackerEOA)` for each ERC20 held by the wallet.
5) All wallet token balances are transferred to the attacker, stealing accumulated fees.

prediction.overall_explanation: The core RiskEngine code shown is mostly view/pure math and doesn’t expose obvious direct fund-loss paths for untrusted callers. However, the included BuilderWallet system has a critical, directly exploitable bug: `BuilderWallet.init()` is publicly callable and can be called repeatedly, letting any attacker seize `builderAdmin` and then sweep all tokens from any BuilderWallet (which are deterministic fee-recipient addresses). This enables theft of protocol/builder fees without any privileged role compromise.
